nominees.name: Gina Hinojosa
nominees.role: Democratic nominee; Texas state representative (Austin attorney)
team: Chuck Rocha, campaign consultant; Fight Agency, Democratic consulting firm brought in (Texas Tribune).

Coalition strategy per advisers: Latino voters plus suburban and conservative voters upset about public education (Texas Tribune). No campaign manager, chief of staff or transition lead named in the sources opened.

positions.stance: Ends the voucher-style education savings program, raises teacher pay, fully funds neighborhood schools, ends state takeovers of elected school boards, pauses A-F ratings tied to STAAR and changes standardized testing. Says per-student funding is about $10 billion behind 2019.
Would replace Commissioner Mike Morath with an educator; says she would fire him on her first day.
$1,500 payment per household from the Economic Stabilization Fund, about $17 billion by campaign estimate; would cut the fund to about $10 billion. Needs two-thirds of both chambers.

Ends what she calls corporate welfare and uses the savings to cut property taxes; opposes Abbott's plan to eliminate homestead school property taxes. Pitches cash back for renters and broader tax reform that lowers rates for families.

Moratorium on new data center permits until protections for water, power and local input exist; end their tax breaks. Wants Flock cameras taken down and residents refunded; sued in Travis County for Abbott-Musk emails.
Strengthen grid resilience, hold utilities to reliability standards, support energy diversity; criticizes Abbott's handling of Winter Storm Uri.
Affordability agenda aimed at corporate insurers and drug companies; points to high uninsured rates. Her position on Medicaid expansion and abortion was not found in the sources opened.

Supports border security with modern infrastructure at ports of entry and coordination with federal partners; opposes withholding public-safety grants from Austin and Houston; says crossings are now very low.
Says she opposes a state income tax; Abbott cites her 2019 vote against the constitutional ban.

policyShifts.shift: Replace the TEA commissioner, pause A-F ratings and rework STAAR accountability, end state takeovers, redirect funding to teacher pay, smaller classes and special education.
policyShifts.lever: mixed (commissioner is a governor appointment; takeover and testing rules are statute)

policyShifts.shift: Repeal the ESA voucher program (about $1 billion).
Draw $17 billion from the Rainy Day Fund for household payments and cut the fund to about $10 billion.
Fund relief by ending corporate incentives instead of Abbott's sales-tax swap.
Permit moratorium, end tax breaks, remove Flock cameras; release Abbott-Musk emails.
Reverse grant threats against cities; shift to funding local law enforcement.
Attack on no-bid contracts and voucher spending as a 'corruption tax'; expect procurement and contract reviews.

impediments.title: Republican Legislature
impediments.detail: House 88 R / 62 D; Senate 18 R / 11 D with 2 vacancies (Ballotpedia, Nov. 2026). Senate presided over by Dan Patrick, House led by Speaker Dustin Burrows. She says she would rely on outside public pressure.

impediments.title: Two-thirds vote for the $1,500 payments
impediments.detail: The Rainy Day Fund spend needs two-thirds of both chambers; the article says it is unknown whether that support exists.

impediments.title: Patrick's competing 2027 agenda
impediments.detail: Property-tax 'Operation Double Nickel' (another $40,000 homestead exemption), grid security, human-services fraud and 'Sharia' charges; none overlap with her education and data-center agenda.

impediments.title: Independently elected statewide officials
impediments.detail: Lieutenant Governor, Attorney General, Comptroller and Land Commissioner are elected separately and are not under the governor.

impediments.title: Voucher program is law
impediments.detail: Repeal needs the Legislature; the program funds about $1 billion and has a Republican-backed constituency.

impediments.title: Thin mandate and money gap
impediments.detail: Abbott spent nearly $100 million on ads vs about $16 million; about 20% of likely voters said they didn't know enough about her; polls mixed.

impediments.title: Income-tax attacks
impediments.detail: Abbott campaign ties her to a state income tax, citing her 2019 vote against the constitutional ban; voters approved the ban.

impediments.title: Fund size and rules unclear
impediments.detail: Sources give the Rainy Day Fund as $24.8 billion (KSAT) and $28 billion (Forward Times); the structure of the payments depends on legislation.

insights: Expect her agenda to split into what the governor controls alone (TEA commissioner, appointments, contract reviews, executive directives, vetoes and special-session power) and what needs a Republican Legislature (vouchers, Rainy Day Fund, data-center rules). The first group is where early action will be.

Most of her fiscal ideas collide with Patrick's, which centers on larger homestead exemptions. The overlap is property-tax relief; she would have to pitch relief paid by ending corporate incentives instead of by exemption growth or an Abbott-style sales-tax swap.
School finance is the likeliest bipartisan space: she cites past work with rural Republicans against vouchers and says she wants 'bipartisan space for public schools.'

Advisory exposure: moratorium and tax-break rollbacks on data centers affect power, water and local-incentive planning; renewed scrutiny of Abbott-era contracts affects procurement and compliance work; ESA repeal affects school-district and TEA operations.

analysis.assumption: Scenario: assumes Gina Hinojosa wins the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. AP had not called this race when checked (Nov. 4, 2026 04:08 UTC). Not a call or forecast.
analysis.summary: A Democratic governor facing a Republican supermajority-style structure: Republicans control both chambers and the presiding officers, and four statewide executive offices are independently elected. The early window is executive: appoint a new TEA commissioner, fill hundreds of board and commission seats as terms expire, review contracts and Abbott-era initiatives, and use vetoes and special-session calls. Anything that needs spending the Rainy Day Fund or repealing vouchers needs Republican votes.
analysis.timing: Inauguration expected mid-January 2027 and the regular legislative session begins in January 2027 (dates as recalled; verify). Ballotpedia lists no regular session in 2026.
priorities: Affordability: $1,500 household payments from the Rainy Day Fund (TPR, KUT).
Public schools: end vouchers, replace the TEA commissioner, pause A-F ratings (KSAT, KUT).
Data-center moratorium and end of their tax breaks (TPR, KBTX).
Property-tax relief funded by ending corporate incentives (KUT, KBTX).
firstMoves: Name a chief of staff, general counsel and budget lead (none identified; analyst inference).
Name a TEA commissioner and begin the A-F pause (stated; see sources).
Open talks with Dan Patrick and Speaker Burrows on school finance and property tax (inference from her stated bipartisan-space goal).
Order contract and procurement reviews of Abbott-era deals (inferred from her no-bid contract criticism).
risks: Republican control of both chambers and Patrick's competing agenda.
Two-thirds threshold for Rainy Day Fund spending.
Senate confirmation of key appointees (rule not verified in sources opened).
Texas lacks a statewide Democratic bench in other executive offices.
analysis.pollContext: Polls were tight; one Marist poll had Abbott ahead by 4, a late-July Fox poll by 1, and five public polls showed him trailing (Texas Tribune). Not a forecast.

nominees.name: Greg Abbott
nominees.role: Republican nominee; incumbent governor seeking a fourth term
team: Not researched for staff or advisers.

positions.stance: Eliminate school property taxes for homeowners and raise the sales tax to pay for it.

Champions the education savings account program; wants districts to send at least 70% of funding to classrooms, limits on classroom devices, tougher penalties for teachers convicted of abuse; summer tuition discounts at four-year universities.
Border security emphasis; threatened to withhold about $2.5 million in public-safety grants from cities that limit police-immigration cooperation.
Announced measures to rein in Flock cameras and data-center development (Texas Tribune).

insights: Continuity case: policy extends the 2023-2027 agenda; the transition question is personnel and the fourth-term agenda, not direction.
